concept.name: Arithmetic mean
concept.definition: The sum of a set of values divided by their count; the most common measure of central tendency (location). It is the value that minimizes the sum of squared deviations from the data.
concept.intuition: It is the 'fair share' value: if every observation were replaced by the mean, the total would stay the same. It balances the data like a center of gravity.
concept.mechanics: Add all observations and divide by the number of observations. Every value, including extremes, contributes fully, which makes the mean efficient for well-behaved data but sensitive to outliers.
concept.formula: x_bar = (1/N) * SUM_{i=1..N} x_i, where x_i are the observations and N is their count.
concept.failure_modes: Extreme tail values can pull the mean far from the bulk of the data (NIST illustrates this with Cauchy data, where the mean is useless as a location estimate). For multiplicative processes such as compounded returns, the arithmetic mean overstates the actual growth rate.
concept.misconceptions: The arithmetic mean is not always the 'typical' value: for skewed distributions like income or returns it sits above the median. Averaging periodic returns arithmetically does not give the compounded growth rate - that requires the geometric mean.
concept.example: Monthly returns of +5%, -3%, and +7% have arithmetic mean (5 - 3 + 7)/3 = 3% per month; the compounded monthly growth is slightly lower at the geometric mean of about 2.9%.
